one_liner: Research C code doing 8 Montgomery multiplications or modexps at once with AVX512-IFMA; ~4-5x GMP/OpenSSL throughput.
what_it_does: Computes batches of eight independent Montgomery multiplications, squarings and constant-time fixed-window modular exponentiations for operands of 260 to 4154 bits. It is benchmark-oriented research code (IACR CIC 2024 paper), not a library. Each directory (Montgomery/, WindowExponentiation/, SBClassicMultiplicationSquaring/, IFMA256/ModExp/, Openssl_RSA_Z_512/) builds its own main with a Makefile. Inputs are 64-bit limb arrays that must be converted with expand()/contract() into a 52-bit word-sliced batch layout.
how_it_is_fast: Operands are held in radix 2^52 and word-sliced, so lane i of each 512-bit register holds one word of operand i; VPMADD52LUQ/HUQ then do eight 52x52-bit multiply-adds per instruction. The 'truncated' Montgomery reduction skips computing low-order product words that are known to cancel to zero, which the paper reports saves about 21% over the non-truncated variant. Schoolbook multiplication is used up to 4108 bits and Karatsuba (double Karatsuba at 4154 bits) above that. Each operand size gets its own code: a script includes a size-specific source file (e.g. sb512_1040.c) at build time.
when_to_use: You have many independent modular multiplications or exponentiations with the same bit size, e.g. batched RSA/DH private-key operations or batch signature work, and can group them in eights.
Your CPU has AVX512-IFMA (Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Zen 4 or later) and you want throughput, not single-operation latency.
Operand sizes from 1024 to 4096 bits, where the paper measures 3.3-5.4x over GMP mpn_sec_powm and OpenSSL BN_mod_exp_mont_consttime.
You are studying or prototyping IFMA Montgomery kernels and want a reference for the truncated-reduction trick.
when_not_to_use: You need a single modexp at a time: the speedup comes from 8-way batching, and a batch of one still costs a full batch.

You already use OpenSSL 3's IFMA path (BN_mod_exp_mont_consttimex2): the margin falls to 1.75x at 1024 bits and 1.38x at 2048, and the 256-bit-vector batch-of-4 variant is only 1.05x faster at 2048 bits.
You need general big-integer arithmetic (add, divide, GCD, arbitrary sizes): only Montgomery mul/sqr/modexp at compile-time-fixed sizes are provided.
The CPU lacks AVX512-IFMA (older Intel, Zen 3 and earlier, ARM): the paper notes NEON has no 52-bit multiply-add equivalent and no fallback exists.
You need GPL-incompatible licensing or a maintained API: GPL-3.0, 7 commits, no releases, benchmark mains rather than a library interface.

integration.dependencies: GMP and OpenSSL libcrypto (linked by the benchmark Makefiles for baselines and tests); libm
integration.min_toolchain: GCC with AVX512-IFMA intrinsics (paper used GCC 9.4.0, -O3 -funroll-all-loops -march=native)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX512F + AVX512-IFMA required; Linux assumed (rdtsc/rdpmc benchmarking)

gotchas: Operand size is a compile-time macro (SIZE) and script.sh rewrites a source include per size, so each size needs a separate build.
Converting between 64-bit limbs and the 52-bit sliced format costs extra; the paper reports conversion overhead separately, and it is not included in the headline cycle counts.
Measured on a laptop with Turbo Boost off; AVX512 frequency effects on other CPUs are acknowledged but not characterized.
The GMP baseline is eight sequential mpn calls; GMP has no batched API, so the comparison is throughput-vs-latency by design.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over ctbignum or mp++ only for batched fixed-size modular exponentiation on AVX512-IFMA hardware, a case they do not vectorize; for general mpz-style arithmetic use mp++ or FLINT, and for small fixed-limb compile-time arithmetic use ctbignum.
verified_claims_summary: On an i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake, Turbo off), GCC 9.4.0 -O3 -march=native, a batch of 8 truncated Montgomery multiplications ran 5.34x/4.86x/3.95x faster than 8 GMP 6.2.0 calls at 1024/2048/4096 bits, and batched fixed-window modexp ran 3.98x/3.71x/3.30x faster than OpenSSL 3.2.1 BN_mod_exp_mont_consttime. Against OpenSSL's IFMA consttimex2 path the gain is 1.75x (1024) and 1.38x (2048).
status_note: Stale research code (last commit 2024-09-19, 3 stars) under GPL-3.0; copyable if GPL fits, but expect to extract kernels from benchmark mains yourself.
